q.oq: Were the Master and senior officers familiar with the company procedure for maintaining the vessel’s statutory certification up to date, were all certificates and documents carried onboard up to date and was the vessel free of conditions of class or significant memoranda?
q.p: Are all certificates up to date and tracked properly, and is the ship free of class conditions or memoranda?
q.w: Expired or missing certificates mean the ship may not be legally fit to trade, and open class conditions show unresolved defects.
c: The company procedure for tracking certificate validity
A few certificates picked at random (up to five) against your tracking list
Whether any condition of class, memoranda or short-term certificate exists
That any class-related defects are in the defect reporting system
That the latest class survey results appear in the class status report
rd: Company procedure for managing certificates and supporting documents
Folders of statutory and class certificates with survey and test reports
Certificate index showing every expiry date
Class Survey Status Report (CSSR) or class status report
List of open defects from the defect reporting system
Record of class attendance in the last twelve months
x: No clear procedure for indexing and filing certificates
Officer cannot explain how certificates are indexed and tracked
A class or flag certificate, or a supporting survey report, expired or missing
Index not kept up to date as the procedure says; class status report not available onboard
Dates in the questionnaire do not match the class report
Any condition of class, memoranda or short-term certificate
q.s: Our SMS has a procedure that tells us how to index, file and track every certificate. I check the index against the folders, and any survey or class finding goes into the defect system. Electronic certificates are controlled in the same way through our SMS.

pr.q: How do you make sure no certificate expires without you knowing?
a: We keep a certificate index with every expiry date
Index is reviewed as per company procedure
Surveys are planned ahead with class and company

pr.q: Do you have any conditions of class or memoranda?
a: Check the latest class status report and answer honestly
Explain that each item is in the defect system
Show the plan and dates for close-out

q.tip: Before the inspection, compare the class status report line by line with your certificate index so the dates match.

q.oq: Had the vessel been attended by a company Superintendent at approximately six-monthly intervals and were reports available to demonstrate that a systematic vessel inspection had been completed during each attendance declared through the pre-inspection questionnaire?
q.p: Did a company superintendent inspect the ship about every six months, with a full report for each visit?
q.w: Regular visits by shore staff give the company a true picture of the ship's condition and how onboard management is working.
c: Inspection reports for each visit in the last eighteen months
That each report covers all operational and accessible areas
The gaps between inspections by marine and technical superintendents
That defects and weaknesses from reports were followed up to closure
Remote inspection procedure and reports, if used
rd: Full report copy for every qualifying superintendent visit in the last eighteen months
Proof defects went into the defect reporting system
Proof procedural weaknesses went into the non-conformity process
Company remote inspection procedure, if remote inspections were used
x: A report for a declared visit is not onboard
Report format does not cover all areas of the ship; more than seven months between inspections
More than fourteen months since the last marine or technical inspection
New ship with no inspection since handover
More than one remote inspection when a physical visit was possible
Findings not followed up as defects or non-conformities
q.s: The company sends a marine or technical superintendent about every six months. We keep the full report from each visit onboard. Every defect goes into our defect system and procedural points go through the non-conformity process until they are closed.

pr.q: When was the last superintendent visit and what did he find?
a: Give the date and the main findings
Show the report onboard
Show how each item was followed up

pr.q: How are findings from superintendent reports tracked?
a: Defects go into the defect reporting system
Procedural issues go through non-conformity reports
Items stay open until closed with evidence

q.tip: Keep the last eighteen months of reports in one folder with a simple list of dates, so you can hand it over in one go.

q.oq: Were recent ISM internal audit reports available on board, had corrective action been taken on board to close-out any non-conformities and had this corrective action been verified by shore management?
q.p: Are recent internal ISM audit reports onboard, and were non-conformities closed and checked by the shore office?
q.w: Internal audits show whether the ship really follows its SMS, and closing findings properly stops the same problems coming back.
c: The company procedure for scheduling and carrying out internal audits
The latest two internal audit reports under the current operator
The system that tracks non-conformities until closed
Whether the Master or a senior officer understands the audit process
rd: Company procedure for internal ISM audits with standard formats or checklists
Latest two internal audit reports
Non-conformity tracking records with time limits and close-out dates
Evidence behind each close-out, such as photos or superintendent visit notes
If the ship is new to the company, the plan for the first audit
x: No procedure for scheduling and doing internal audits
No internal audit for more than 15 months, or over 12 months with no reason recorded
Last two audit reports not onboard; tracking records incomplete or not available to those responsible
No time limit set for corrective action; no record of the operator verifying the close-out
Non-conformity open past its time limit or closed with no evidence
Master or senior officer does not know the audit process
q.s: Internal audits are done at least every twelve months under a company procedure with standard checklists. Each non-conformity has a time limit, and when we finish the corrective action, the office verifies it and closes it out. Our two latest reports are here.

pr.q: How do you close out an audit non-conformity?
a: Do the corrective action within the time limit
Report completion to the company
Company verifies with evidence and records final close-out

pr.q: When is the next internal audit due?
a: Give the date from the audit programme
Twelve months maximum, up to three months more only in exceptional circumstances
Know where the schedule is kept

q.tip: Attach photos or the superintendent's note to every closed item. 'Done' without evidence is a common finding.

q.oq: Was the Master fully conversant with the company’s Safety Management System and had Master’s Reviews of the system taken place in accordance with the ISM Code and company procedures?
q.p: Does the Master know the SMS well, and are Master's reviews done as the ISM Code and company procedure require?
q.w: The Master's review feeds real feedback from the ship back to the company so the SMS keeps improving.
c: Whether the Master knows the layout of the SMS and can find things quickly
The last two Master's reviews
The company replies to those two reviews
The company procedure for the review: format, agenda, frequency, reply time
rd: The SMS in hard copy or digital form
Last two Master's reviews, fully completed
Company responses to both reviews
Company procedure for Master's review
x: Master not familiar with the layout and contents of the SMS
Master cannot find information in the SMS quickly; no company procedure for the periodic review
Reviews not done at the frequency the procedure sets
Review not completed to the company format or agenda
Review lists no deficiencies or improvement suggestions, just ticks
Company did not reply within the set time
q.s: I know how our SMS is laid out and can find any procedure quickly. I do the review at least once a year using the company format, and I include real deficiencies and suggestions. Here are the last two reviews and the company replies.

pr.q: How often do you review the SMS and what do you include?
a: At least annually, whole SMS within twelve months
Deficiencies and corrective action proposals
Suggestions to improve the SMS, with input from officers and safety committee

pr.q: Show me how you find the procedure for a given task.
a: Go straight to the right section
Show you can use hard copy or digital version
No need to know every detail by heart

q.tip: Write specific, useful comments in your review. Inspectors can tell when it is only a tick box.

q.oq: Were the Master and Chief Engineer familiar with the company procedure to maintain the Enhanced Survey File in accordance with Classification Society rules, and was the vessel free of any visible or documentary evidence of concerns with the structural condition of the hull or cargo and ballast tank coatings?
q.t: Structural concerns and Enhanced Survey File
q.p: Is the Enhanced Survey File kept up to date, and is the hull, cargo and ballast tank coating free of structural concerns?
q.w: Hidden hull damage, corrosion or failed coating can lead to structural failure and pollution, so full records and a good physical condition matter.
c: The Enhanced Survey File and whether all required sections are complete
Repair history in the last twelve months against the defect reporting system
Condition evaluation report for fair or poor coating, heavy corrosion or deep pitting
Coating Technical File for recorded repairs
Visible cracking, denting, distortion or serious wastage while walking round
rd: Enhanced Survey File, including survey reports, condition evaluation and thickness reports
Coating Technical File where required
Survey programme, main structural plans and repair history
Ship staff inspection reports for cargo, ballast and void spaces
Incident investigation reports linked to structural damage or repair
x: No procedure to keep the Enhanced Survey File or Coating Technical File current; officer cannot explain how the file is maintained
Required surveys or reports missing from the file; ship staff inspections not recorded
Structural repair in the survey file but no defect report; structural repair after an incident with no incident investigation report
Fair or poor coating, or heavy corrosion or deep pitting, in class reports
Ballast tank coating repairs not entered in the Coating Technical File
Cracks, dents, distortion or wasted structure with no class survey
q.s: Our company procedure tells us how to keep the Enhanced Survey File and Coating Technical File up to date as class requires. Every repair is recorded in the file and also in our defect system. Ship staff tank inspections are recorded and kept with the file.

pr.q: What is in the Enhanced Survey File?
a: Survey, condition evaluation and thickness reports
Survey programme, structural plans, repair history
Ship staff inspections and the Coating Technical File where required

pr.q: When coating repairs are done in a ballast tank, what do you record?
a: Update the Coating Technical File
Keep it onboard for the life of the ship
Link it to the maintenance plan

q.tip: Cross-check the last twelve months of structural repairs in the survey file against the defect system before the inspection.

q.oq: Were the Master and Chief Engineer familiar with the company procedure to maintain the Class Survey File, and was the vessel free of any visible or documentary evidence of concerns with the structural condition of the hull or hold space and ballast tank coatings?
q.t: Structural concerns and Class Survey File
q.p: Is the Class Survey File complete and current, and is the hull, hold space and ballast tank coating free of structural concerns?
q.w: Gas carrier structure and ballast tank coatings must be tracked closely so damage and deterioration are found and repaired early.
c: The Class Survey File: class status reports, survey reports, repair history
Repair history in the last twelve months against the defect reporting system
Coating Technical File, where required, for recorded repairs
Survey reports for heavy corrosion, deep pitting or poor coating
Visible cracking, denting, distortion or serious wastage on the ship
rd: Class Survey File, complete and current
Coating Technical File where required
Ship staff inspection reports for cargo, ballast, hold and void spaces
Incident investigation reports relevant to structural damage and repair
x: No procedure to keep the Survey File complete; master or Chief Engineer unfamiliar with that procedure
Survey File missing class status reports, survey reports, repair history or coating file
Coating maintenance not part of the maintenance plan; structural repair in the file but no defect report
Structural repair after an incident with no investigation report
Fair or poor ballast coating, or heavy corrosion or pitting, in reports
Visible structural damage with no occasional class survey
q.s: Our company procedure covers keeping the Class Survey File complete and up to date. Repairs are recorded in the file and in the defect system, and ballast coating maintenance is in our planned maintenance. Coating repairs go into the Coating Technical File where required.

pr.q: What does your Survey File contain?
a: Class status reports and survey reports
Repair history
Coating Technical File where required

pr.q: How do you handle structural damage found by the crew?
a: Enter it in the defect reporting system
Inform company and class
Record the repair in the file and investigate any incident

q.tip: Check that any repair you list in the Survey File also has a matching defect entry.

q.oq: Were the Master and senior officers familiar with the company cargo, ballast & void space inspection and reporting procedure and, were records available to demonstrate that all inspections had been accomplished within the required time frame with reports completed in accordance with company instructions?
q.t: Cargo, ballast and void space inspection
q.p: Are cargo, ballast and void spaces inspected on time, and are reports made in the company format?
q.w: Regular inspections find corrosion, coating failure and leaks before they become structural damage or pollution.
c: The company procedure: frequencies, actions if an inspection is late, report format
Inspection reports for the full previous cycle, spot-checked against the dates declared
That each report records the detail the company form asks for
That defects found were entered into the defect reporting system
Extra inspections where class conditions, memoranda or coating condition required them
rd: Company inspection procedures and any referenced industry guidance
Inspection reports for all cargo, ballast and void spaces for the last full cycle
Open defect reports for tank structure, coatings or fittings
Communications with class about tank structure defects
Enclosed space entry permits and records for recent inspections
x: Procedure does not give clear frequency, process and reporting criteria
Ballast or void space frequency longer than twelve months
Oil or chemical cargo tank frequency longer than thirty-six months
Any space overdue by more than a month against company period; a space left out of the inspection regime
Report form cannot record coating and structural condition by area
Defects in reports not moved to the defect system; tank structure defects not reported to class
q.s: Our procedure sets the frequency for each type of space. Ballast tanks, voids, pipe trunks and cofferdams are inspected yearly. Cargo tanks are inspected about every two and a half years on oil and chemical ships. Reports follow the standard form and any defect goes into the defect system.

pr.q: How often do you inspect each type of space?
a: Ballast, void, pipe trunk, cofferdam: annually
Oil and chemical cargo tanks: 2.5 years, six-month window either side
Gas carrier hold spaces: annually

pr.q: What does your inspection report record?
a: Structural deterioration, corrosion, pitting and coating condition
Leaks, equipment condition and sediment
Defects are passed to the defect system

q.tip: Keep a simple tracker of last and next inspection date for every space, so you can show nothing is overdue.

q.oq: Were the Master and deck officers familiar with the company procedures for detecting leakage of liquids between cargo, bunker, ballast, void and cofferdam spaces which included inspecting the surface of ballast water prior to discharge, and were records available to show that the necessary checks had been performed?
q.t: Monitoring spaces for leakage and contamination
q.p: Do deck officers know how to detect leaks between cargo, bunker, ballast, void and cofferdam spaces, and are checks recorded?
q.w: Undetected leaks between tanks can contaminate ballast and cause oil pollution when it is discharged.
c: Company procedures for sighting ballast surface before discharge
Sounding records for empty spaces
Ballast discharge records showing surface checks on at-risk tanks
Records of ballast line tests through cargo or fuel tanks
Whether ballast tank sighting arrangements are easy to use
rd: Procedure for sighting ballast surface before discharge
Procedure for periodic sounding of empty spaces and level checks on full tanks
Records of surface checks, soundings and level checks
Records of ballast line tests where lines pass through cargo or fuel tanks
x: No procedure to check empty spaces for liquid coming in or to check ballast surface
Officer unfamiliar with the procedures; soundings of empty spaces not done as the procedure requires
Ballast surface not inspected before discharge from tanks next to cargo or bunker tanks
Ballast lines through cargo or fuel tanks not tested
Sighting needs many bolts removed or an enclosed space entry
Leakage in an empty space, or oil in ballast, in the last twelve months
q.s: Before discharging ballast from tanks next to cargo or bunker tanks, or with oil lines passing through, we sight the surface and record it. We sound empty spaces regularly and check levels in full tanks. If we find contamination or liquid migration, we follow the company procedure.

pr.q: What do you do before discharging segregated ballast?
a: Sight the surface of tanks next to cargo or bunker tanks
Also tanks with oil or hydraulic lines passing through
Record it, and follow procedure if contaminated

pr.q: How do you detect liquid moving between spaces?
a: Periodic soundings of empty spaces
Periodic level checks in full tanks
Ballast line tests where they pass through cargo or fuel tanks

q.tip: Make sure sighting ports can be opened quickly, because heavy hatches suggest nobody ever checks them.

q.oq: Had the vessel been enrolled in a Classification Society Condition Assessment Programme (CAP)?
q.p: If the ship has a class CAP rating, are the dates and ratings declared correctly and the certificate available?
q.w: A CAP rating gives charterers an independent view of the ship's condition, so the information given must be accurate.
c: CAP certificate against the date and module ratings declared in the questionnaire
The survey completion date, not just the certificate issue date
Any records that support the certificate
rd: CAP certificate showing survey completion date and rating for each module
Evidence of onboard survey dates if certificate shows only issue date
Supporting information or records for the certificate
x: Information in the pre-inspection questionnaire is wrong
Rating claimed for a module still pending completion
Certificate issue date declared as the survey date
Certificate not uploaded and not onboard
q.s: Our CAP certificate is available onboard. The survey dates and module ratings match what the company declared. CAP is voluntary and the rating shows the ship's condition on the day of the survey.

pr.q: What does your CAP certificate cover?
a: Modules assessed and the rating for each
Dates of the onboard survey
Rating reflects condition on the survey date

q.tip: Check the survey completion date on the certificate. It is often different from the issue date.

q.oq: Were the senior officers familiar with the company procedure for reporting defects to vessel structure, machinery and equipment to shore-based management through the company defect reporting system and was evidence available to demonstrate that all defects had been reported accordingly?
q.p: Do senior officers know how to report defects to shore, and have all defects been reported?
q.w: Unreported defects stay hidden from management, so repairs are delayed and risks are not controlled.
c: The company defect procedure and how officers use it
Entries in the system: timely, sent ashore and acknowledged
A sample defect with a repair timeline and any interim measures
Any obvious defect seen during the inspection that is not in the system
rd: Company procedure for managing defects
The defect reporting system or planned maintenance system if combined
Shore acknowledgement of each defect entry
A printed list of all open defects, marking those reported to class or flag
x: No defect reporting system or procedure
Senior officer unfamiliar with the procedure
Defects not acknowledged by shore management
Visible defects on listed or class items with no defect report
Defect that caused, or was caused by, an incident not reported as an incident
q.s: Under our procedure, all defects to structure, machinery, navigation, deck, cargo and electronic equipment go into the defect system. Shore management acknowledges each one and sets a repair timeline. I have printed the list of open defects for you, with class or flag notifications marked.

pr.q: What happens when you find a defect?
a: Enter it in the defect system within the company time limit
Shore acknowledges and sets a corrective timeline
Mitigating actions if safety is affected

pr.q: What if a defect caused an incident?
a: Also submit an incident report
Follow the company incident procedure
Investigation and follow-up

q.tip: Print the open defect list before the inspector arrives and walk the deck and engine room yourself looking for defects that are not on it.

q.oq: Where defects existed to the vessel’s structure, machinery or equipment, had the vessel operator notified class, flag and/or the authorities in the port of arrival, as appropriate to the circumstances, and had short term certificates, waivers, exemptions and/or permissions to proceed the voyage been issued where necessary?
q.t: Defect reporting to class, flag and others
q.p: When defects exist, did the company tell class, flag or the port as needed, and were short-term certificates or waivers issued?
q.w: Defects that affect class or statutory equipment must be disclosed so the ship is not trading without proper approval.
c: Class status report for conditions of class, memoranda or short-term certificates
Open defects that should have been reported to class or flag
Pre-arrival notices where a short-term certificate or waiver applies
That any conditions set by class or flag were complied with
rd: Company procedure for notifying class, flag and other parties
Class status report
Defect system with a printed list of open defects, class and flag reports marked
Shore messages saying the defects were assessed and what was reported
Class or flag letters with mitigating conditions, and port pre-arrival notices
x: No procedure for shore to decide if class, flag or others must be told
Senior officers do not know the procedure
Significant open defect with no proof that class or flag were informed
Class or flag conditions imposed but no evidence they were met
q.s: Under our procedure, shore management assesses each defect to decide who must be told: class, flag or the port. For any short-term certificate or waiver, we follow the conditions set and keep the messages onboard. Port pre-arrival notices are made when required.

pr.q: Who decides if class or flag must be informed of a defect?
a: Shore management evaluates under company procedure
Procedure says what, when and by whom
Records of notifications are kept onboard

pr.q: What do you do if flag gives a waiver with conditions?
a: Follow every condition
Keep the records
Inform the port of arrival if required

q.tip: Keep all class and flag correspondence for a defect in one folder next to the defect entry.

q.oq: Had the company Management of Change procedure been effectively implemented for changes affecting structure, machinery and equipment governed by Classification Society rules or statutory survey?
q.p: Is the company Management of Change procedure followed for changes to class or statutory structure, machinery and equipment?
q.w: Unplanned changes to the ship can create new risks, so each one needs approval, risk assessment and updated documents.
c: The company MOC procedure
Changes declared in the last twelve months in the pre-inspection questionnaire
The MOC register or index onboard
The request, risk assessment and documents for any recent change
Any recent change you can see on board that was not declared
rd: Company MOC procedure
MOC register or database index
MOC request form for every change in the last twelve months
Supporting papers: risk assessments, training plans, updated drawing lists
x: No MOC procedure for class or flag regulated changes
Senior officer cannot explain the MOC process
A change in the last twelve months not declared in the questionnaire
A change made with no approved MOC form and supporting documents onboard
q.s: Our MOC procedure says which changes need approval and which, like for like replacement, are excluded. Each change has a request, shore approval, risk assessment and updates to affected drawings and procedures. All of them are indexed in our MOC register.

pr.q: What counts as a change that needs MOC?
a: Changes to structure, machinery or equipment under class or statutory rules
New installations or modifications
Like for like replacement is usually excluded

pr.q: What happens after a change is approved?
a: Tell the people affected
Update drawings, manuals and checklists
Confirm updates are done and file the records

q.tip: Walk round before the inspection looking for anything new or modified, and check each one has an MOC file.

q.oq: Were the Master, deck officers and engineer officers familiar with the vessel’s Ballast Water Management Plan and were records available to demonstrate that ballast handling had been conducted in accordance with the plan?
q.p: Do officers know the Ballast Water Management Plan, and do records show ballast was handled as the plan says?
q.w: Ballast water can spread harmful organisms and, if mishandled, can also stress the hull or pollute.
c: The approved Ballast Water Management Plan and the BWM Certificate
Ballast water record book entries against the plan
Cargo and ballast plans and records of ballast timings
The exchange plan with stresses, draughts and trim, if exchange was done
Messages to flag and port if the treatment plant failed
rd: Ship-specific approved BWM Plan in the working language
International Ballast Water Management Certificate
Ballast Water Record Book, up to date
Recent cargo and ballast plans
Exchange sequence plan showing stresses, if exchange was done
Notifications and replies if treatment could not be used
x: No plan or no valid certificate
Plan not approved by flag or class, or not ship specific
Responsible officer does not know the plan
Plan not in the working language of the ship; record book not kept to company procedure
No sequential exchange plan with longitudinal stress
Ballast treatment plant defective in any way; treatment plant bypassed against the plan
q.s: Our plan is ship specific and approved, and the BWM Certificate shows our main method. We record every ballast operation in the record book. If the treatment plant fails, we inform flag and port and follow any conditions they give.

pr.q: Who is responsible for the plan and what must they know?
a: The officer named in the plan
Contents of the plan and record book entries
What to do if the plan cannot be followed

pr.q: What if the ballast treatment plant breaks down?
a: Follow company procedure
Tell flag and port state
Comply with any conditions they impose

q.tip: Check your record book entries against cargo and ballast plan times. Mismatches stand out quickly.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the VOC Management Plan, and had the procedures for minimising VOC emissions set out in the Plan been implemented and documented as required?
q.p: Do officers know the VOC Management Plan, and are its steps to reduce VOC emissions followed and recorded?
q.w: Crude oil cargo releases harmful vapour, so the plan aims to keep emissions as low as practical.
c: The VOC Management Plan
Records of cargo operations and tank pressures during the voyage
That the cargo plan includes the plan's requirements
VOC training records
The target tank pressure shown in the cargo control room
rd: Approved ship-specific VOC Management Plan in a language the officers understand
Training records for the plan
Records of loading, carriage, discharge and crude oil washing as the plan requires
Current cargo plan
Deck logbook
x: Plan not approved or not ship specific; plan not in a language the Master and officers understand
Responsible person does not know the plan
Accompanying officer unaware of what the plan needs during current cargo operation
No evidence of training or of procedures used
Target operating pressure not shown in the cargo control room
Tank pressure kept well below target by venting to atmosphere
q.s: Our VOC plan names the person responsible and sets a target tank pressure, which is displayed in the cargo control room. We follow it for loading, carriage, discharge and crude oil washing, and keep the required records. The cargo plan includes the plan's requirements.

pr.q: What is the target pressure for the cargo tanks?
a: State the value from the plan
Explain it is kept as high as safely possible
If venting is needed, lower the pressure as little as possible

pr.q: What does the plan ask you to do on this operation?
a: Follow the loading and carriage steps in the cargo plan
Keep the required records
Consider crude oil washing effects

q.tip: Put the target pressure on a clear label in the cargo control room and quote it from memory.

q.oq: Were the Master and senior officers familiar with the contents and requirements of the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) and had these been fully implemented?
q.p: Do the Master and senior officers know the SEEMP, and have its energy saving and fuel reporting steps been carried out?
q.w: The SEEMP cuts fuel use and emissions, and fuel data must be collected and reported correctly each year.
c: The SEEMP, Part I and Part II
Evidence that the Part I energy saving measures were carried out or monitored
Records of fuel data collection, aggregation and reporting
Statement of Compliance for fuel oil consumption reporting
Whether the Master or Chief Engineer knows the plan
rd: Ship-specific SEEMP
Logbook evidence of measures: voyage planning, speed, trim, hull maintenance
Annual fuel consumption, distance and hours underway records
Evidence of reporting to the flag administration
Statement of Compliance - Fuel Oil Consumption Reporting (5,000 GT and above)
x: Master or Chief Engineer does not know the SEEMP; part I has no ship-specific package of measures
No evidence the measures were carried out or monitored
Part II does not describe how fuel data is collected and reported
No Statement of Compliance issued
Fuel records leave out boilers, inert gas generator or other consumers
Fuel records not split by fuel type
q.s: Our SEEMP Part I lists ship-specific measures such as voyage planning, weather routeing, speed and trim, and hull maintenance. Part II describes how we collect, total and report fuel use for all consumers. We keep the records and have the Statement of Compliance.

pr.q: Which fuel consumers are included in your records?
a: Main and auxiliary engines, boilers, inert gas generator, any others
Each fuel type recorded separately
Counted whether underway or not

pr.q: What energy saving measures do you apply?
a: Name the measures in the SEEMP Part I
Show how they are applied and monitored
Point to the log entries that prove it

q.tip: Make sure the Chief Engineer and Master can both name three or four SEEMP measures and where the proof is kept.

q.oq: Was the relevant content of the SMS manuals easily accessible to all personnel on board in a working language(s) understood by them?
q.t: SMS content available to all crew
q.p: Can everyone onboard easily get the SMS content they need, in a language they understand?
q.w: A procedure nobody can find or read does not protect anyone.
c: The SMS manuals in hard copy or electronic form
Evidence that changes to the SMS were told to the right people
Easy access to navigation procedures on the bridge
Versions of checklists and procedures in use
A random rating: can they find and understand the SMS relevant to them
rd: SMS manuals, current and relevant to this ship
Records of SMS changes being communicated and understood
Navigation procedures on the bridge, with backup power if electronic only
Enough hard copies, or workstations and training for electronic access
x: Manual hard to navigate or slow to use
Large parts not relevant to the ship, such as other ship types
Too few hard copies in the right places; electronic only, but not everyone has access or training
Navigation procedures not on the bridge, or electronic with no backup power
Old copies not updated, or old checklists still in use
A rating cannot access or understand the SMS part for their job
q.s: Our SMS is available to everyone in a language they understand, and the navigation procedures are on the bridge. When the SMS changes, we brief the crew and keep a record. Old copies are removed so only current versions are in use.

pr.q: How do you tell the crew about a change in the SMS?
a: Brief the people affected promptly
Make sure they understand
Keep a record

pr.q: (To a rating) Where do you find the procedure for your job?
a: Know the way to access it
Be able to read it in your language
Ask your supervisor if unsure

q.tip: Check every checklist copy has the same revision number as the SMS before the inspector arrives.

q.oq: Did the SMS identify clear levels of authority and lines of communication between the Master, ship's officers, ratings and the company, and were all onboard personnel familiar with these arrangements as they related to their position?
q.t: Authority and lines of communication, including the DPA
q.p: Does the SMS show clear authority and communication lines, and does everyone know their own and who the DPA is?
q.w: In an emergency or a safety concern, people must know who decides and who to call ashore.
c: The SMS chart or text showing authority and communication lines
A senior officer: do they know key shore contacts including the DPA
A junior officer or rating: do they know who the DPA is, how to reach them and what the role is
rd: SMS section on authority and communication lines, charts or flowcharts are fine
DPA name and contact details displayed or given to all
List of key shore contacts for navigation and technical matters
x: SMS does not clearly show authority and communication lines
Senior officer unfamiliar with key shore contacts
Junior officer or rating does not know who the DPA is, contact details or role
q.s: Our SMS shows the chain of authority from Master to officers to ratings and the company, with the Master's overriding authority on safety. Everyone onboard knows the DPA's name, contact and role. Senior officers also know the superintendent and navigation contacts ashore.

pr.q: Who is the DPA and how do you contact them?
a: Give the name and role

q.sec: DP & Shuttle Tanker Specialist Procedures and Equipment

Two independent differential satellite systems

Report as company procedure says
Investigate and close out actions

Paint, solvents, oil or wood stored in machinery space or steering gear room
Lagging missing, damaged or soaked in oil
Oil leaks, waste oil in bilges or save-alls, rubbish in bilges
Floor plates removed with open holes, or loose and uneven
Guards missing, spare gear or tools left near switchboards, batteries or steering rams
Gauge glass closing devices inhibited, or sounding caps missing
Fire doors held open with wedges or hooks
Broken lights, missing signs, pipelines not colour coded or labelled
q.s: The designated Safety Officer inspects the machinery spaces at the interval in our procedure, using the company checklist. We look at leaks, lagging, guards, bilges, floor plates and fire doors, and we record and close each finding. I can show you any item on the checklist.

pr.q: Why must fire doors to the steering gear room not be tied open?

Machinery space fires are a high risk
Wedges, hooks and tiebacks are not approved

Free from oil
Particularly near oil systems

pr.q: What would you check around the bilges and tank tops?
a: No waste oil built up
Painted light colour to show leaks
No rubbish blocking the mud boxes

q.tip: Do your own walk-round the day before, starting at the steering gear and ending in the purifier room. Check fire doors, floor plates and gauge glasses first.
ref: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices 5.5 and 20

Wet or dirty bilges, or cargo drained to the pumproom bilge
Leaks from pumps, lines or glands, or bandage repairs on pipes

Lower suctions open

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the procedure for safety inspections of the cargo machinery rooms, and had inspections been effective in identifying hazards to health, safety and the environment?

Continue throughout operations
Run also if a leak is suspected

Lighter or heavier than air
Officer must know their location and status

Galley oil fires, lint in dryers, damp stored linen

Safety chains on open vertical ladders

q.oq: Were the Master, officers and ratings familiar with the company lifting and rigging procedures, and was evidence available to demonstrate that each item of lifting and rigging equipment had been maintained, inspected and tested in accordance with the procedure?

Needs examination before use again

a: Identify parts that could fail
Decide the minimum spares
Keep the crane working after one failure

Same specification and rating

With communication to the bridge
Escorts the pilot by a safe route

Report any defect before use

q.oq: Were the Master, deck officers and deck ratings familiar with the company procedures for rigging the accommodation ladders, and were the accommodation ladders in good order and used in accordance with the company procedure and manufacturer’s instructions?

Report defects before use

q.oq: Were the Master, officers and crew familiar with the escape routes from the machinery spaces, pump rooms, compressor rooms, accommodation spaces and, when in port, from the vessel, and were these routes clearly marked, unobstructed and well illuminated?

q.oq: Were the Master, officers and ratings familiar with the company procedures that addressed the use of respiratory protective equipment during cargo operations, and did the procedures prohibit the use of filter type respirators for this purpose?

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedure for maintaining the Cargo Record Book, and did the entries contained in the Cargo Record Book accurately record the cargo related operations required to be documented by MARPOL Annex II?

Entries not signed by the officer in charge, or pages not signed by the Master

Prewash entry not endorsed by the port authority inspector
Washings discharged to sea against MARPOL Annex II
Annex I cargo operations written in the CRB instead of ORB Part II

q.p: Do officers know how to run the BWMS safely, and is it working and used as per procedure and maker's manual?

c: Company procedure and maker's operation and safety manual
Control panel: system operational, no faults or alarms
Self-monitoring data from the last ballast operation
Unit intact, not modified or bypassed
Chemical stock, storage and handling if used
rd: Procedure naming who supervises and who may operate the BWMS
Maker's operation and safety manual
Maintenance and inspection records in the plan
Operation records for each ballast operation
Enclosed space procedure posted for the BWMS room
x: No procedure covering hazards, chemicals, by-products and failure actions
Officer does not know hazards or what to do if the BWMS fails
No maintenance records in the plan or no operation records
Pumps, filters or back-flush not working
Self-monitoring data shows it did not work properly last time
BWMS modified or bypassed, or not enough chemicals, or poor chemical storage
q.s: Our SMS says who supervises and who may operate the BWMS, and lists the hazards and controls. We follow the maker's manual, keep operation and maintenance records, and know the actions if it fails. Chemicals are stored and handled as per the procedure.

pr.q: What hazards does the BWMS present?
a: Toxic or flammable gas, such as hydrogen from electrolysis systems
Chemicals used for disinfection or neutralisation
Treatment room treated as an enclosed space

pr.q: What do you do if the BWMS fails?
a: Follow the failure actions in the company procedure
Know these actions before the operation starts
Record the failure

q.tip: Check the BWMS room entry notice matches your enclosed space entry procedure, or you collect a second observation under 5.5.1.

q.oq: Were the Master, officers and ratings familiar with the company procedures for the removal of small quantities of oil or chemical spilled and contained on deck, and was suitable response equipment available, in satisfactory condition and effectively deployed?
q.t: Main deck oil or chemical spill clean up equipment
q.p: Do crew know how to clean up small spills on deck, and is the equipment ready, in good order and used well?
q.w: A small deck spill must be contained and cleaned quickly so it never reaches the sea or becomes a fire risk.
c: SOPEP or SMPEP and company procedure for deck spills
Inventory of spill equipment and inspection records
Equipment at the manifold, quantities match the inventory
Dump valves or other disposal means aft on both sides
Portable pump demonstrated, and a rating asked about equipment and PPE
rd: SOPEP or SMPEP and spill procedure
Inventory kept by a designated officer, with periodic checks
Instructions for safe use including PPE
Non-sparking scoops, shovels, buckets, sorbents, scupper plugs
Portable pump bonded, fixed down, with air ready
x: No inventory, or inspection records missing, or quantities differ from the inventory
Equipment missing at the manifold or in short supply
Scoops or buckets not non-sparking
Portable pump not bonded, not secured, no air, or hose through a sighting port
Dump valves would not drain, or limits not posted
No spill tank or drip tray under each manifold connection, or an unbonded plastic tray
q.s: Our spill equipment is kept at the manifold and listed in an inventory kept by a designated officer, with periodic inspections. The crew are trained and know the PPE for the cargo carried. The portable pump is bonded and ready, and recovered waste is disposed of as per our procedure.

pr.q: A small spill happens at the manifold. What do you do?
a: Stop the operation and raise the alarm
Contain it with scupper plugs and sorbents
Remove with non-sparking tools and pump, then dispose properly

pr.q: Rating: where is the spill kit and what PPE do you wear?
a: Know the location of the equipment
Use PPE required for the cargo being handled
Know what each item is for

q.tip: Ratings are asked this question directly, so run a quick spill kit talk with the deck team before the inspection.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the disposal of accumulations of water contaminated with oil and/or marine pollutants in the forecastle and other internal spaces, and had the procedures been implemented?
q.t: Disposal of oily water in the forecastle and other internal spaces
q.p: Do officers know how to dispose of oily or polluted water collected in the forecastle and similar spaces?
q.w: Oil from a hydraulic leak in a bilge well must not go overboard and must be traceable.
c: Company procedure for bilge wells in internal spaces
Records of disposals
Bilge wells in forecastle, pumproom and steering gear
How levels are monitored and how unauthorised discharge is prevented
Pollution notices and secured overboard valves where pumps or ejectors fitted
rd: Procedure listing spaces, minimising waste, monitoring, disposal and records
Disposal records for any past leaks
Notices posted and overboard valves secured
Bilge wells clean and checked
Pump testing in the maintenance plan
x: No procedure or officer does not know it
Evidence of a leak but no record of how it was disposed of
Disposal arrangements or discharge prevention inadequate
Bilge well with a significant amount of oil or pollutant
Spaces not identified in the procedure
q.s: Our procedure lists the spaces with bilge wells, how levels are checked and how oily water is disposed of. Every disposal is recorded. Where pumps are fitted, overboard valves are secured and notices are posted.

pr.q: What if you find oily water in the forecastle bilge well?
a: Find and stop the source
Dispose ashore or to a proper tank, never overboard
Record how it was disposed of

pr.q: How do you stop accidental discharge?
a: Overboard valves secured
Pollution notices posted
Regular inspection of bilge levels

q.tip: Look in the forecastle bilge well the day before: a small hydraulic leak with no record is a classic finding.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the emergency arrangements to pump out the machinery space bilges in the event of flooding, and were these arrangements prominently marked and in good order?
q.t: Emergency arrangements to pump out the machinery space bilges
q.p: Do engineers know how to pump out a flooded engine room, and are valves marked and in good order?
q.w: In a flooding the engine room must be pumped out fast, without misuse of the emergency suction for daily bilges.
c: Company procedure for emergency bilge pumping
Emergency bilge suction valve accessible and clearly marked
Valves marked, and which pump to start is shown
Warning signs on emergency overboard valves, and seals
Engineer explains sequence for sea water pipe failure and other flooding
rd: Procedure and machinery space flooding emergency plan
Marked valves and suction, pump indication
Warning notices posted
Numbered easily breakable seals recorded in log or ORB Part I
Valves free to operate, not seized
x: No procedure or no flooding emergency plan
Engineer cannot explain the valve and pump sequence
Emergency suction not accessible or not marked
No warning notice on emergency overboard valve
Seals missing, not as procedure, or not easily breakable
Evidence emergency discharge used for daily bilge disposal
q.s: Our procedure covers the bilge pumps, direct suctions and the emergency bilge suction. Valves are marked and sealed with numbered breakable seals recorded in the log. I can explain the sequence for a sea water pipe failure and for other flooding. The emergency line is never used for daily bilges.

pr.q: The engine room is flooding. What do you do?
a: Follow the flooding emergency plan and procedure
Line up the emergency bilge suction and overboard valves in the sequence in the procedure
Start the pump marked for the emergency suction
Break the seal and inform the bridge

pr.q: Can you use this line for daily bilge disposal?
a: No, emergency use only
MARPOL exceptions: to secure ship safety or save life, or after damage to ship or equipment
Seal numbers recorded

q.tip: Know which pump serves the emergency suction and be able to point to it without looking at the drawing.

q.oq: Were the engineer officers familiar with the company procedure for the safe use of the incinerator, and was the incinerator in satisfactory condition and used in accordance with the company procedure and in compliance with MARPOL?
q.p: Do engineers know how to use the incinerator safely and legally, and is it in good order?
q.w: Burning the wrong waste breaks MARPOL and creates fire, fume and health risks.
c: Company procedure and risk assessment for safe incinerator use
Operating instructions posted at the controls
List of items not to be incinerated posted in the space
Loading chute interlocks working and not bypassed
Engineer explains PPE, loading, emergency stop and prohibited items
rd: Procedure and risk assessment
Operation and maintenance manual
Prohibited items list posted
Separated waste stored for disposal ashore
Clean incinerator space with no waste piled up
x: No procedure or no risk assessment
Engineer unsure about PPE, loading, prohibited items or failure actions
Incinerator out of service or defective; no instructions or prohibited list posted
Overheated casing, fume leaks, or oil dripping around casing; interlocks defective or bypassed
Burning in places or times where MARPOL, local rules or company procedure forbid it
Waste left to pile up around the space
q.s: Our procedure says who may use the incinerator, when it must not be used, and what may and may not be burned. The risk assessment covers the chute interlocks. Instructions and the prohibited items list are posted at the incinerator, and I know the PPE and emergency stop.

pr.q: What must you never burn in the incinerator?
a: Cargo residues and PCBs
Exhaust gas cleaning residues
PVC unless in a type-approved incinerator
Items on the posted prohibited list

pr.q: When is incinerator use not allowed?
a: Where MARPOL, local rules or company procedure forbid it
Sludge in ports, harbours and estuaries

q.tip: Test that the interlock really prevents the chute opening while the furnace is hot, as far as possible with the unit stopped.

q.oq: Were the Master and engineer officers familiar with the company procedures for the use of the oil filtering equipment, and was the oil filtering equipment in satisfactory condition and used in accordance with the company procedure, manufacturer’s instructions and MARPOL Annex I?
q.p: Do engineers know how to use the oily water separator, and is it working, sealed and used per MARPOL?
q.w: Bilge discharges must stay within MARPOL limits, and tampering or misuse means illegal pollution.
c: Company procedure for use of the oil filtering equipment
Overboard valve closed, secured and sealed with a warning sign
Flanges and connections sealed with no signs of tampering
15 ppm alarm calibration certificate
Engineer demonstrates alarm, automatic stopping device and recorder using the test facility
rd: Procedure and maker's manuals
Bilge alarm calibration certificate
Maintenance records in the plan
Oil Record Book Part I with any out-of-service entries
Bilge alarm data kept as the procedure says
x: No procedure, or officer cannot explain the restrictions and fault actions
Alarm not calibrated within five years or the maker's period if shorter
Overboard valve open, unsealed or no warning sign
Signs of tampering or unsealed flanges; equipment defective, or no maintenance records
Engineer cannot demonstrate alarm, stopping device or recorder
Out of service with no Oil Record Book Part I entry
q.s: Our procedure says who may use the separator and when overboard discharge is allowed. The overboard valve is locked and sealed, with the key held as per procedure. I can demonstrate the alarm, stopping device and recorder, and any breakdown is entered in the ORB Part I.

pr.q: The separator breaks down. What do you do?
a: Stop use and follow the company procedure
Record time out of service and returned in ORB Part I
Retain bilges onboard or land ashore

pr.q: What if you find a flange or pipe has been tampered with?
a: Report to Chief Engineer and Master
Follow the company procedure
Do not use the equipment

q.tip: Practise the test facility demonstration before the inspector asks, including the recorder print-out.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the use of the oil discharge monitoring and control system, and was the oil discharge monitoring and control system in satisfactory condition and used in accordance with the company procedures, manufacturer’s instructions and MARPOL Annex I?
q.t: Oil discharge monitoring and control system (ODME)
q.p: Do officers know how to use the ODME, and is it working and used as per procedure, maker and MARPOL?
q.w: ODME keeps discharges from cargo and ballast spaces within MARPOL limits and records them.
c: Company procedure for ODME use and authorisation
Control panel with no faults or alarms
Printout or stored data legible and available
Speed, position and GMT time inputs correct
Records for any manual-mode discharge and failures
rd: Procedure and maker's manuals
Maintenance and test records
ODME printouts or downloadable data
Oil Record Book Part II and bridge logbook
Written shore approval if any manual mode discharge was done
x: No procedure or officer does not know manual mode and fault actions
System defective, modified or extra connections added
Maintenance and testing not as maker and procedure say
Manual mode discharge with no shore management approval
Printout illegible or data not available
Out of service with no ORB Part II entry
q.s: Our procedure covers who may operate ODME, checks before and after discharge, lookouts and what to do if it fails. We keep the printouts and enter everything in the ORB Part II. Manual mode is never used without approval from shore management.

pr.q: ODME fails during discharge. What do you do?
a: Stop the discharge
Record the defect in ORB Part II
Inform shore management and get approval before any manual mode

pr.q: What if the lookout sees a slick astern?
a: Stop the discharge immediately
Inform the bridge and Master
Follow the pollution emergency plan

q.tip: Check the speed, position and GMT time on the ODME panel are correct before the inspector looks.

q.oq: Was security threat and risk assessment an integral part of voyage planning, and did the passage plan contain security related information for each leg of the voyage?
q.t: Security threat and risk assessment during passage planning
q.p: Is security risk assessed in voyage planning, and does the passage plan carry security information for each leg?
q.w: Piracy and armed robbery risks must be planned for before entering an area, not met by surprise.
c: Security charts and BMP or regional guidance on the bridge
Passage plan and security risk assessment for a recent voyage
Security notes on each leg, reporting points, speed, bridge manning
Review of the assessment before entering an increased risk area
Bridge security cards or checklists
rd: UKHO or equivalent security charts
BMP and regional guidance such as ReCAAP
Passage plan, appraisal form and risk assessment for a completed voyage
Company advice on routeing, speed, waiting areas
Bridge logbook and bridge security cards
x: Security charts or BMP publications missing
No security risk assessment for a recent voyage
Assessment lists no ship protection measures where needed
No company routeing guidance for a high-risk transit
Assessment not reviewed or plan not updated before entering the area
Passage plan has no security information for each leg; bridge security cards missing
q.s: We do a ship-specific threat and risk assessment for every voyage, using current security charts, BMP and company guidance. The passage plan marks security levels, reporting points, extra lookouts and speed. We review it before entering an increased risk area. The security plan is confidential, so I will describe it only in general.

pr.q: What security information is in your passage plan?
a: Reporting points such as entering a VRA
Bridge manning, speed and day or night transit
Security level changes and hardening points

pr.q: When do you review the risk assessment?
a: Before entering an area needing higher vigilance
Update the passage plan if needed

q.tip: If the company tells you not to report to a VRA, annotate the plan so the reporting points are shown as not to be used.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for hardening the vessel when entering areas of increased security risk, and was there a Vessel Hardening Plan (VHP) available?
q.p: Do officers know how to harden the ship for areas of increased security risk, and is there a Vessel Hardening Plan?
q.w: Hardening makes it much harder to board the ship, but it must not block escape routes or lifesaving gear.
c: Company procedure and ship-specific Vessel Hardening Plan (VHP)
VHP lists materials and quantities needed
Inventory of hardening materials against stock onboard
Maintenance records for water cannons, CCTV, cameras
Security officer explains the plan, LSA and FFA stay accessible
rd: Vessel Hardening Plan, which can sit in the SSP
Inventory of hardening materials
Inspection and maintenance records for security equipment
Records of past implementation such as logs, work plans, photographs
Safety guidance for rigging razor wire and working near the ship's side
x: No procedure or no VHP
VHP not ship-specific, or lacks materials list and quantities
No inventory, or inventory does not match actual stock
No maintenance records for security equipment
No record that the VHP was implemented before the area
Security officer not familiar with the plan
q.s: Our VHP is specific to this ship and lists the materials and quantities needed. We keep an inventory and maintain the security equipment. When hardened, lifeboats, life rafts and firefighting gear stay clear. The security plan is confidential, so I can show the cover and review date.

pr.q: What does the VHP include?
a: Ship-specific measures and materials list with quantities
Inventory and when materials are kept onboard
Maintenance of security equipment
Safety guidance for rigging

pr.q: What must hardening not interfere with?
a: Escape routes
Lifesaving appliances and firefighting equipment
Response to non-security emergencies

q.tip: Count the hardening materials against the inventory before the inspection, since a mismatch is easy to spot.

q.oq: Were the Master, officers and ratings familiar with the company procedures to control access to the vessel in port and to ensure the safety of visitors, and were these procedures effectively implemented?
q.p: Do crew control who comes onboard in port and make sure visitors know the hazards and safety rules?
q.w: Unchecked visitors are a security risk, and visitors who do not know the hazards are a safety risk.
c: Gangway watch continuous and watchman knows the procedure
Visitor photo ID, passes, log, escort to accommodation
Notice board at the gangway with warnings
Visitor information card or briefing on hazards and rules
Deck patrols for unauthorised access points such as hawse pipes and mooring ropes
rd: Access control procedure, in or outside the SSP
Visitor log with entries in and out
Visitor passes and information cards
Gangway notice board with warnings in suitable languages
List of approved visitors sent to the terminal, including the SIRE inspector
x: No continuous gangway watch, or watchman unfamiliar with procedure
No list of approved visitors given to the terminal
No deck patrols, or CCTV not monitored
No photo ID, passes or visitor records
Visitors not escorted or baggage not searched per security level
No notice board, or visitors not briefed on smoking, phones, PPE, cargo hazards, emergency signals, drug and alcohol policy
q.s: We keep a continuous gangway watch, check photo ID, issue passes and log every visitor. Visitors are escorted and given an information card on hazards, PPE, smoking, phones and emergency signals. We patrol the deck for other access points and gave the terminal our approved visitors list.

pr.q: Gangway watch: what do you do when a visitor arrives?
a: Check photo ID and approved list
Issue a pass and record in log
Brief on hazards, give PPE if needed, and escort

pr.q: What else do you watch besides the gangway?
a: Hawse pipes and mooring ropes
CCTV where fitted
Regular deck patrols

q.tip: Brief the gangway watchman on exactly what the visitor card says. He is the first person the inspector meets.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with regional maritime security reporting requirements and operation of the ship security alert system (SSAS) and had this equipment been regularly tested?
q.p: Do the Master and officers know the regional security reporting rules and how the SSAS works, and is it tested?
q.w: Authorities can only help if they know where you are and your alert system works when needed.
c: 24-hour contact details of the Company Security Officer, posted
Master and SSO know voluntary reporting procedure for VRAs
SSAS, LRIT and any standalone security comms regularly tested
Officers know where the SSAS buttons are and how it works
Whether VRA reporting was considered in passage planning
rd: CSO name and 24-hour contacts posted
Records of voluntary security reporting
Test records for SSAS and LRIT kept per the SSP
Passage plan marking VRA reporting points
Annotations if company told you not to report
x: Officer does not know the CSO 24-hour contacts, or not posted
Master or SSO not familiar with VRA reporting procedure
No evidence VRA participation considered in planning
Company required reporting but no reports made; no records of regular SSAS or LRIT testing
Officer cannot explain purpose and operation of SSAS or LRIT
Security communication equipment defective
q.s: The CSO name and 24-hour contacts are posted on the bridge. We consider VRA reporting at passage planning and report as our procedure requires. SSAS and LRIT are tested regularly and I know where the activation buttons are.

pr.q: Where are the SSAS buttons and what do they do?
a: Know all locations
Send a covert alert to company and authorities
Used in a real security threat, not casually

pr.q: How do you report in a VRA?
a: Register and report to the centre as company procedure says
Continue reports while transiting
Or annotate plan if company says not to report

q.tip: The inspector will not ask you for equipment details, so know purpose and operation, not just that tests are done.

q.oq: Did the Ship Security Officer (SSO) have a valid Certificate of Proficiency and a full understanding of their role, and were ship security records of port calls being maintained as required by SOLAS?
q.p: Does the SSO hold a valid certificate, understand the role, and are security records for port calls kept?
q.w: A trained SSO and proper port call records show security is actually run onboard, not just written down.
c: SSO Certificate of Proficiency, valid
SMS names the SSO and lists the role and duties
SSO is a crew member, not an outside consultant
Evidence of regular security inspections by the SSO
Security records for the last 10 port calls, and a rating's knowledge of security procedures
rd: SSO Certificate of Proficiency
SMS section on ship security with SSO duties
Records of regular security inspections
Port call security records for last 10 calls
Contact details of the CSO
x: SMS does not clearly name the SSO or list the duties
SSO certificate not valid, or SSO is not a crew member
SSO unsure of the SSP purpose, equipment testing, hardening plan, CSO or PFSO role
Rating knows nothing about security procedures or alarm response
No evidence of regular security inspections
Port call security records not kept for the last 10 calls
q.s: Our SMS names the SSO and lists his duties. I hold a valid Certificate of Proficiency. I carry out regular security inspections and keep the records for the last 10 port calls. The security plan itself is confidential, but I can explain my role and who the CSO is.

pr.q: What are your duties as SSO?
a: Regular security inspections and keeping the SSP up to date
Security awareness, training and drills
Make sure security equipment is tested and maintained
Report incidents and liaise with CSO and PFSO

pr.q: What security records do you keep?
a: Records for the last 10 port calls
Security level and any special measures taken
Inspection and drill records

q.tip: Brief ratings on the alarm signal and their first action, because the inspector may ask one of them.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for cyber security risk management, and had these procedures been fully implemented?
q.p: Do officers know the company cyber procedures, and are they actually in place onboard?
q.w: A cyber incident can take out navigation, cargo or propulsion systems, so protection and a backup plan must be real.
c: Company cyber risk procedures and the officer responsible onboard
Register of sensitive IT and OT systems
Locked spaces and secured USB or network ports
Control of admin profiles, passwords, portable media and visitor access
Hard copy cyber contingency plans and IT support contacts
rd: Cyber risk management procedure
Inventory of sensitive IT and OT systems
Approval records for technicians and remote access
Cyber training records
Printed contingency plans and IT support contact details
x: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it
Spaces with sensitive equipment unlocked, or USB ports open
No inventory of IT and OT systems; admin profile held by someone other than a senior officer
Passwords posted at workstations, no password needed, or shared at crew change
Anti-virus or patches not updated, or portable media not scanned offline
No contingency plans or no hard copy; no approval for a technician working on ECDIS or similar
q.s: Our procedure names who is responsible for cyber risk onboard and lists our IT and OT systems. Only senior officers hold admin profiles, passwords are changed regularly, and USB ports are secured. We have printed contingency plans and IT support contacts if systems are lost.

pr.q: A technician wants to update the ECDIS. What do you do?
a: Get formal approval before access
Supervise the work
Record the access
Check media offline for malware

pr.q: What if you lose GNSS or navigation data?
a: Use the contingency plan
Revert to other position fixing and backups
Inform company IT and shore support

q.tip: Keep the contingency plan printed at the bridge, not only on a computer that may be the target.
ref: Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships v4

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the use of the inert gas system, and had the inert gas system been used in accordance with ISGOTT guidance, with cargo tanks maintained in an inert condition at all times, except when it was necessary to be gas-free for entry?
q.t: Inert gas system usage on oil tankers
q.p: Do officers know the IG procedures, and are cargo tanks kept inert at all times except when gas-free for entry?
q.w: Inert tanks cannot burn or explode, so any lapse in IG use puts the whole ship at risk.
c: Company procedure for IG operation
Oxygen in the IG main at 5 percent or less
Tank pressure within the range in the cargo and ballast plan
Oxygen in a random tank less than 8 percent
Cargo, tank cleaning and gas freeing records for last three months
rd: IG procedure and instruction manuals
Cargo and IG records for three months or three voyages
Positive pressure of at least 100 mm WG maintained
Portable oxygen analyser working
Failure action steps known
x: No procedure, or officer cannot explain IG failure actions
IG not in use when required
Tanks below 100 mm WG, or pressure outside plan values
IG main oxygen over 5 percent, or tank over 8 percent
No periodic oxygen checks
Records missing or show IG not used per procedure
q.s: We keep cargo tanks inert at all times except when gas-free for entry, with at least 100 mm WG pressure. Oxygen is not more than 5 percent in the IG main and not more than 8 percent in the tanks. If IG fails, we stop discharge, close the deck isolating valve, open the vent and repair.

pr.q: What do you do if the IG system fails?
a: Stop cargo and ballast discharge from inerted tanks
Close the IG deck isolating valve and open the vent valve
Repair immediately and report as required

pr.q: How do you gas free a tank?
a: Purge with IG until hydrocarbon is below the critical dilution line
Never pass through the flammable range

q.tip: Know the oxygen reading in the main and in a tank at any time, since the inspector may ask you to measure.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures and international regulations for the planning, preparation, conduct and documentation of crude oil washing operations (COW), and was the COW system in satisfactory condition and used in accordance with the company procedures for each COW operation?
q.p: Do officers know how to plan, prepare, run and record COW, and is the COW system in good order?
q.w: COW is risky: a leak, wet oil or too much oxygen can cause fire or static explosion.
c: Company procedures and the COW manual
COW plan, checklists, SSSCL and records for current or last operation
Oxygen tested in each tank within 30 minutes before COW and at 8 percent or less
Pressure gauges, lines, machines and heater blanked if outside engine room
Person in charge explains procedures and qualification
rd: COW manual approved and updated for any changes
Completed COW checklists and plan
Records: tanks, machines, start and end times, pattern, pressure, how dry
Evidence line pressure tested and checked for leaks before arrival
Oil Record Book Part II
x: No procedure, or PIC unfamiliar or not suitably qualified
No approved COW manual, or manual not updated after alterations
Oxygen above 8 percent, or not tested within 30 minutes; records or checklists incomplete
Leaks, defective gauges, or machines turning in tanks not being washed
Source tank not de-bottomed 1 m, slop tank not discharged first
Heater not blanked, hydrants not capped, or washing cycles not as the manual says
q.s: Our procedure covers roles, planning, checklists and records. We test oxygen in each tank within 30 minutes before washing and it must not be more than 8 percent. We pressure test the line before arrival, use dry crude, blank the heater and watch the line for leaks throughout.

pr.q: What checks before COW starts?
a: Oxygen tested in each tank at 8 percent or less
Line pressure tested and leak checked
Tank cleaning heater blanked, hydrants capped
Checklists completed

pr.q: Why use dry crude?
a: Oil and water mist builds higher static charge
De-bottom source tank by 1 m
Fully discharge slop tank before using it as source

q.tip: If no COW is planned, the inspector uses your last record, so keep that file complete.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the isolation of individual cargo tanks from the common venting system in accordance with SOLAS, and were these procedures being followed?
q.t: Cargo tank isolation from venting system
q.p: Do officers know how to control the isolating valves between each tank and the common vent line?
q.w: A wrongly set isolating valve can over or under pressurise a tank and damage the structure.
c: Company procedure for isolating valves
Record or display of the current valve status
Valves on deck: correct position, locked, visibly indicated
Records of tests, maintenance and pre-operation checks
Officer explains who may operate them
rd: Isolation procedure
Status record or display at the CCR matching actual valve positions
Locks controlled by the Responsible Officer
Maintenance and pre-operational test records
Authorised personnel list
x: No procedure or officer unfamiliar with it
Valve incorrectly set, or status differs from the record
No record or display of valve status
Valve not locked, or locks not under the Responsible Officer
No maintenance, testing or pre-operation check records
No clear visual indication of position; anyone allowed to operate valves
q.s: Each tank isolating valve has a lock under the Responsible Officer's control and a clear position indication. We record valve status in the CCR and check it before every operation. Only authorised persons operate them, and they are tested and maintained.

pr.q: Why isolate a tank, and what must you check before cargo or ballast?
a: Isolating valves are opened before loading, ballasting or discharging that tank
Check status against the record
Locks under the control of the responsible officer

pr.q: What can cause over pressurisation?
a: Incorrect valve setting
Failure of an isolating valve
Casual operation of valves

q.tip: Walk the deck and compare every valve with the CCR status board before the inspection.

q.oq: Were the Master and deck officers familiar with the company procedures for planning and documenting cargo tank cleaning operations after the carriage of volatile products, and had these procedures been followed?
q.p: Do deck officers know how to plan, run and record tank cleaning and gas freeing after volatile cargoes?
q.w: Tank cleaning and gas freeing are among the most hazardous tanker jobs, so every step must be planned and supervised.
c: Company tank cleaning and gas freeing procedures
Plans, risk assessments, logs and records for recent cleaning
Tank washing done in an inert atmosphere
Supervision by a Responsible Officer and crew briefing
Special methods: steaming, chemicals, slops, purging
rd: Tank washing and gas freeing plans
Risk assessments including any cleaning additives
Logs and records following company procedure
SDS for tank cleaning chemicals
Brief records showing roles and responsibilities explained
x: No procedure, or officer not familiar; no plans or supporting records for recent cleaning
Plan not followed, or cleaning not carefully planned
