Calibration records, fixed system within the last 30 months
Calibration certificates for portable instruments
Cross-check of fixed against portable readings
x: No procedure or no records of checks, tests or calibration
Officer cannot demonstrate the fixed equipment and alarms
Fixed equipment not calibrated within the last 30 months
Not tested and calibrated to manufacturer's instructions, fixed or portable
One or more temperature sensors defective
Visible or audible alarm defective
q.s: Our procedure covers maintenance, testing and calibration to the manufacturer's instructions. I can show the fixed system and its alarms working. Calibration of the fixed system has been done within 30 months and the records are here. We also compare portable and fixed readings as a cross-check.

pr.q: How often is the fixed temperature system calibrated?
a: Per manufacturer's instructions
Preferably not more than 30 months apart
Often done during repair periods

pr.q: How do you check a fixed sensor between calibrations?
a: Compare against a portable instrument
Record the comparison
Report any sensor that disagrees

q.tip: Put the next calibration due date for the fixed system on the planned maintenance calendar so it is never missed.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for managing cargo and vapour connections at the cargo manifolds, and were the manifold arrangements in satisfactory condition?
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures for managing cargo and vapour connections at the manifolds, and are the manifolds in good condition?
q.w: Poorly made-up or unblanked manifold connections are a common source of spills and leaks.
c: Company procedure for managing cargo and vapour connections at manifolds
Manifold connections: full bolting, hose or arm support, pressure gauges
Blanks on unused connections, drains and sample points
Drip trays: present, clean and drained, no covers over gratings
Bow and stern manifolds, vapour manifold keying and marking, platform edge protection
rd: Procedure covering connections, gauges, blanks, drip trays, vapour manifolds, platforms, hose support, crane use, bow and stern manifolds
Documentation for blank flange pressure rating where blanks are not the same thickness
Clean drip trays with working drains, valves capped
Pressure gauge on each connection outboard of the valve, with valve and cap when not fitted
Spray guards for acids or toxic or corrosive cargo on chemical ships
x: Bolts damaged or wrong size, or not a bolt in every hole
Improvised G-clamp or camlocks not fully engaged
Loading arm supported on items not meant to carry load
Cargo hose not properly supported
Unused manifold not blanked, or leaking, or drain or sample point not capped
No drip tray, dirty drip trays, plastic trays not bonded, or manifolds drained into open trays
Midships crane used for stores during cargo, or edge protection missing on high platform
Stern manifold not isolated, or three-metre danger area not marked
q.s: Our procedure covers hose or arm connections, pressure gauges, blanks on all unused connections, drains and sample points, drip trays, vapour manifolds and safe work on the platform. Every flange has a bolt in every hole, and drip trays are clean and drained. Unused lines are blanked, not just closed by valves.

pr.q: Why blank unused manifolds instead of relying on the valve?
a: Valve tightness cannot be relied on
Prevents leaks and seepage
Blanks fully bolted and rated for the line

pr.q: How do you avoid mixing up vapour and liquid connections?
a: Keyed flange with a stud at 12 o'clock
Vapour connections painted or marked
Check at pre-transfer

q.tip: Walk the manifold with the bosun before each cargo and check bolts, blanks, drip trays and gauges as a fixed routine.

q.oq: Were the Master and deck officers familiar with the company procedures for receiving nitrogen from shore for operations such as inerting, purging or padding cargo tank, or for clearing cargo lines?
q.p: Do officers know the company procedure for receiving shore nitrogen to inert, purge, pad tanks or clear lines?
q.w: Shore nitrogen can come at high pressure and flow, and can over-pressurise and damage cargo tanks very quickly.
c: Company procedure for receiving nitrogen from shore
Risk assessments and records from at least one operation in the last six months
Ship shore safety checklist showing agreed procedure, maximum pressure and flow rate
Your knowledge of how the incoming flow is controlled
Whether flammable-cargo lines were cleared to the ship with nitrogen, not compressed air
rd: Procedure covering risk assessment, connection and piping choice, and flow control
Completed risk assessment for each nitrogen receipt
Completed ship shore checklist items on nitrogen, pressure and flow
Records of the latest operation within six months
Plan to pad through the vapour system where possible
x: No procedure for receiving nitrogen for inerting, purging, padding or line clearing
Procedure does not cover risk assessment, connection choice or flow control
Risk assessment not available for a past nitrogen receipt
Checklist did not record agreed pressure and flow rate
Hoses or arms with flammable cargo cleared to the ship using compressed air
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
q.s: Before we take nitrogen from shore we carry out a risk assessment and agree the pressure and flow rate with the terminal on the checklist. We control the incoming flow so it never exceeds what our vents can pass. We pad through the vapour system where possible and never clear flammable lines with compressed air.

pr.q: What is the main danger of shore nitrogen?
a: High pressure and flow can over-pressurise tanks quickly
Flow may exceed P/V valve capacity
Possible structural damage and loss of containment

pr.q: How do you control the incoming flow?
a: Agree pressure and flow with the terminal
Restrict flow to what vents or vapour return can pass
Do not throttle with the manifold valve; use it only as an emergency stop

q.tip: Brief the whole watch at the pre-transfer conference on who watches tank pressure and who can stop the flow.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures that addressed the carriage of inhibited cargoes, and had these procedures been followed?
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures for carrying inhibited cargoes, and were they followed?
q.w: If an inhibited cargo starts to self-react, it can heat up and form solids or explosive peroxides.
c: Company procedure for carriage of inhibited cargoes
Inhibitor certificate with the minimum required information
Cargo logs, temperature records and inert gas logs
Contingency plan for uncontrolled polymerisation
Your knowledge of the procedure, as cargo planning officer
rd: Procedure covering certificates, temperature checks, inerting, reliquefaction draining, anti-freeze, water, recirculation, adding inhibitor, toxicity, contingency
Inhibitor certificate: name and amount, date added and effective life, temperature limits, action if voyage is longer
Daily temperature records of inhibited cargo
Cargo plans for load and discharge
Oxygen records below 0.1 percent for inert gas on vinyl chloride, where relevant
x: No procedure covering all required items
No certificate on board, or certificate missing minimum information
Inhibitor effectiveness period expired before discharge
Temperature not checked at least daily, or as the maker advises
No contingency plan for uncontrolled polymerisation and rapid temperature rise
No records that inert gas oxygen was below 0.1 percent where vinyl chloride was protected by inert gas
q.s: Our procedure covers the inhibitor certificate, temperature monitoring, inerting, purging the reliquefaction system, water exclusion, cargo recirculation and what to do for uncontrolled polymerisation. We would refuse an inhibited cargo without a proper certificate. Temperatures are recorded daily during the voyage.

pr.q: What must the inhibitor certificate tell you?
a: Name and amount of inhibitor
Date added and how long it works
Temperature limits and what to do if voyage is longer

pr.q: What do you do about the reliquefaction system when it is shut down?
a: Drain or purge it with inhibited cargo
Inhibitor may not boil off with the cargo
Prevents self-reaction in the system

q.tip: If no inhibited cargo was carried in the last six months, be ready to say when the last one was and show that record.

q.oq: Were the Master and Officers familiar with the company procedures for carrying out cargo sampling operations?
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures for cargo sampling on an LPG ship?
q.w: Sampling releases cargo near people, so poor equipment or control can lead to exposure, fire or toxic vapour release.
c: Company procedure for sampling every cargo on the Certificate of Fitness
Sampling equipment and connections for compatibility
Marking of sample connections, and whether they are capped when not in use
Sampling in progress, if any, with responsible officer present
Your knowledge of PPE, equipment, connections and locations
rd: Procedure, possibly in the cargo system operation manual
Compatible equipment with correctly marked connections, double valves on liquid samples
Closed-loop equipment for toxic cargoes
PPE and SCBA for toxic cargoes
Certified safe electrical equipment if used
x: Sampling with no responsible officer present
Sample equipment not compatible with connections, or badly connected
Open-loop sampling used on a toxic cargo
No double valves on liquid sampling, or neither valve multi-turn
Inerting or gassing-up connections used for cargo sampling
Missing PPE, or no SCBA for toxic cargo
Sample connection not capped, or vapour-contaminated containers stored in an unventilated space
Plastic vapour bags used for liquid samples
q.s: A responsible officer authorises and directly supervises every sampling job. We use only compatible equipment, minimise venting, purge and ullage containers in a safe place, and use closed-loop equipment with SCBA for toxic cargoes. Connections are marked and capped when not in use.

pr.q: When must closed-loop sampling be used?
a: When sampling toxic products
Open loop may be used for flammable-only cargoes, with release kept to a minimum
Minimise venting always

pr.q: What PPE do you use for sampling?
a: Gloves, goggles and protective clothing for cold cargo
SCBA for toxic cargo
Not just a respirator in an enclosed space

q.tip: Always check the sample container fits the connection before you start. If it does not, any fix must not affect the gastight integrity of the ship's system.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for identifying and segregating incompatible cargoes and refrigerants during cargo stowage planning, and had these procedures been followed?
q.p: Do officers know how to spot and separate incompatible cargoes and refrigerants when planning cargo stowage, and was it done?
q.w: Mixing incompatible cargoes or refrigerants can cause dangerous reactions and contamination.
c: Company procedure for identifying and segregating incompatible cargoes and refrigerants
Compatibility chart from a recognised body, and data used
Current and previous cargo stowage plans
Spool pieces, spectacle flanges or blanks as shown in the stowage plan
Your knowledge of the chart and procedure, as the stowage planner
rd: Procedure covering how to identify, document and achieve segregation
Recognised compatibility chart and safety data sheets
Stowage plans that show where care is needed, which cargoes and the segregation method
Cargo log entries of pipeline isolation before incompatible loading
Segregation drawings in the cargo system operation manual
x: No procedure covering identification, documentation and means of segregation
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure or the chart
No compatibility chart from a recognised body onboard
Incompatible cargoes stowed next to each other without positive segregation
Segregation fitted on the ship not as shown in the stowage plan
Stowage plan not showing when and where to avoid mixing
No cargo log entry of isolating pipelines before loading incompatible cargoes
q.s: Our procedure uses the charterer's instructions, the compatibility chart and shipper's data to identify incompatible cargoes and refrigerants. The stowage plan shows which cargoes are involved and how we segregate them, using spool pieces or blanks. The isolation is logged, and if in doubt we treat cargoes as incompatible.

pr.q: What do you do if you are unsure two cargoes are compatible?
a: Check data sheets and compatibility chart
Seek advice from shippers
If still unclear, treat as incompatible and use positive segregation

pr.q: What is positive segregation?
a: Removable spool pieces or pipe sections
Applies to liquid, vapour and vent lines
Record the isolation in the cargo log

q.tip: Walk the plan on deck: confirm every spool piece and blank shown on paper is actually fitted or removed.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the safe carriage of propylene oxide (PO), ethylene oxide (EO) and PO-EO mixtures?
q.t: Carriage of propylene oxide and ethylene oxide
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures for safely carrying propylene oxide, ethylene oxide and PO-EO mixtures?
q.w: These cargoes are flammable, toxic and self-reactive, so mistakes can lead to fire, explosion or serious exposure.
c: Company procedure, approved cargo handling plans and the P&A Manual
If carried in the last 12 months: segregation certificate, last three cargoes, tank inspection and cleaning records
Records of tank pressure, oxygen, and hold space monitoring
If loaded now: seals on pipeline blanks, and water spray system ready
Your knowledge of the procedure topics
rd: Procedure covering tank preparation, separation of pipelines and compressors, relief valve settings, nitrogen, discharge, vapour return, temperature, hold spaces, sampling, emergencies
Certificate of Fitness or NLS certificate listing these cargoes
Segregation certificate issued by the shore authority before loading
Records of the last three cargoes before PO or EO
Jettison equipment and water spray system in working order
x: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with the topics
Cargo not on the Certificate of Fitness or NLS certificate, no approved handling plan or no P&A Manual
No segregation certificate before loading
Ethylene oxide carried in deck tanks
Pipeline blanks not sealed while handling
Tank pressure not kept above 0.007 MPa gauge during discharge
Hoses not marked 'for alkylene oxide transfer only'
No hold space monitoring records, hold oxygen over 2 percent where inerting required
Water spray not working, no jettison equipment, no cooling system where required
q.s: Our procedure covers tank preparation and compatibility with previous cargoes, separation of pipelines and compressors, nitrogen padding, pressure settings, discharge, vapour return, temperature control, hold space monitoring, sampling and emergencies. We have the segregation certificate, the P&A Manual and approved handling plans, and the water spray system is ready.

pr.q: Why are PO and EO carried under nitrogen?
a: They are self-reactive, especially with air
Cannot be inhibited, so inert gas used
Keep a positive pressure and low oxygen

pr.q: What documents must be on board for these cargoes?
a: Certificate of Fitness or NLS certificate listing them
Approved cargo handling plan
P&A Manual and segregation certificate

q.tip: If your ship is not certified for PO or EO, tell the inspector at the start so the question can be marked not applicable.

q.oq: Were there sufficient escape sets as required by the IGC Code for everyone on board, and did the sets provide suitable respiratory and eye protection?

c: Inspection and maintenance records for escape sets in the maintenance plan
Two escape sets picked at random and inspected
Number of sets against everyone on board while underway, including visitors and contractors
Marking: not for fire-fighting or cargo handling
Rating's knowledge of location, purpose and operation
rd: Sets for every person, in addition to the SOLAS EEBDs in accommodation and machinery spaces
Duration of at least 15 minutes, no filter-type sets, eye protection included
Sets fully charged and marked not for fire-fighting or cargo handling
Company procedure covering use and maintenance
Maintenance records within the planned maintenance system
x: Set duration under 15 minutes, or filter-type protection
No suitable eye protection
Not marked as not for fire-fighting or cargo handling
Not in addition to the SOLAS EEBDs, or not in the procedures and maintenance plan
Set not fully charged, or not inspected as the plan says
Set used for fire-fighting, cargo handling or as the main way to enter unsafe spaces
Too few sets for everyone including contractors and visitors
Rating does not know where sets are or how to use them
q.s: We carry escape sets for everyone on board, in addition to the SOLAS EEBDs. They give at least 15 minutes, include eye protection, and are marked not for fire-fighting or cargo handling. They are in our maintenance plan, and I can show the records.

pr.q: Can you use an escape set to enter a tank space?
a: No, escape only
Not the main way to enter unsafe atmospheres
Not for fire-fighting or cargo handling

pr.q: How many sets do you need?
a: One for every person on board while underway
Include contractors and visitors
In addition to SOLAS EEBDs

q.tip: Update the headcount for the sets whenever supernumeraries or contractors join, so the number never falls short.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the inspection and maintenance of the cargo tank insulation, and was the insulation reported to be in good condition?

Enclosed space entry records for recent insulation inspections
Your knowledge of the procedure
rd: Procedure covering scope, frequency, maintenance, records and fire safety near insulation
Inspection and repair records, maybe within the maintenance plan or hold space inspections
Open defect reports with follow-up action
Enclosed space entry permits for inspections
Hot work precautions covering gas in insulation
x: No procedure covering scope and frequency, maintenance, records and fire safety
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
No inspection, maintenance or repair records
Inspections not done as the procedure says
Defect noted in an inspection but no defect report raised
q.s: Our procedure covers the scope and frequency of insulation inspections, maintenance, records, and fire precautions for any work near the insulation. Inspections are done with enclosed space entry permits and recorded. Any defects found get a defect report for follow-up.

pr.q: What do you check for during an insulation inspection?
a: Condition of insulation and vapour barrier
Signs of moisture or damage
Record defects and raise a defect report

pr.q: What fire precautions apply when hot work is near insulation?
a: Check area for gas in the insulation
Cover exposed insulation with non-flammable material
Insulation may be combustible

q.tip: Link the insulation inspection to your hold space inspection routine so it is never missed.

q.oq: Were the vent outlets from the cargo containment system fitted with the correct protection screen or flame screen required for the cargo being carried, and were the screens in satisfactory condition?
q.t: Vent outlet protection screens or flame screens
q.p: Are the cargo vent outlets fitted with the right protection screen or flame screen for the cargo, and are they in good condition?

c: Cargo records or maintenance plans showing correct screen for the cargo carried

Storage of any flame screens not in use
Flame screens available on board if the ship has an NLS certificate
Carbon dioxide cargo: no screens fitted
rd: Protection screens up to 13 mm square mesh for gas cargoes in general
Flame screens or safety heads for the listed NLS cargoes
Flame screens stored safely and clearly marked so they can be found
Maintenance records showing inspection of screens
Cargo plan showing which screen suits the cargo
x: Wrong or no screen fitted for the cargo
Screen blocked, clogged, painted over or damaged
Flame screens not in use stored badly or not marked
NLS certificate on ship but no flame screens available onboard
Screens fitted on vent outlets while carrying carbon dioxide
q.s: Our cargo plan shows which screen goes on the vent outlets for each cargo. Flame screens go on for the listed NLS cargoes and the coarse protection screens are used otherwise. We never paint screens, and unused flame screens are stored and marked so they are easy to find.

pr.q: Which screen do you fit for normal LPG cargoes?
a: Protection screen, not more than 13 mm square mesh
Stops foreign objects entering
Must not hinder vent flow

pr.q: What is different for carbon dioxide?
a: No flame screens or protection screens on vent outlets
Cargo may solidify and block
Follow the IGC Code requirement

q.tip: Before loading an NLS cargo, check the flame screens are actually onboard and fit the mast, not just listed.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the operation, testing and calibration of the custody transfer measurement system (CTMS), and was the system in satisfactory condition?

Manufacturer's manuals

Your knowledge of the procedure
rd: Procedure covering pre-arrival checks, servicing and periodic calibration

Service and calibration records
x: No procedure for operation, testing and calibration

No records of pre-operational tests, or no test before the current operation
System defective in any way

pr.q: What does the CTMS do?
a: Takes level, temperature, pressure, trim and list readings

Gives the official record of quantity transferred

pr.q: When is the CTMS calibrated?
a: As the company procedure requires

In-service verification can be done at mid-cycle

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the operation, inspection, maintenance and testing of the Gas Combustion Unit (GCU)?

Space ventilation, gas and fire detection, and flame screens on vents or bleed lines
rd: Procedure covering who supervises, hazards, controls, failure in auto mode and manual operation

Inspections, tests or maintenance not done as required

q.s: Our procedure says who supervises the GCU, the hazards and how we control them, and what we do if automatic mode fails, including manual operation. a: Burn excess boil-off gas safely

Handles gas when it cannot be used as fuel or reliquefied

pr.q: What alarms do you test on the GCU?
a: Flame failure, loss of combustion or cooling air
BOG inlet and exit gas temperature, high-high at 535 degrees C
Methane in gas duct, duct ventilation or nitrogen pressure

q.tip: Make sure the GCU is left in automatic mode, as the guidance expects, and know how to take over manually.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the inspection, maintenance and testing of the safety arrangements for the LNG gas fuel supply system, and were these arrangements in satisfactory condition?
q.t: LNG gas fuel supply system safety arrangements

q.sec: Gas (common to all vessels under IGC Code)
q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the maintenance, testing and setting of the independent cargo tank high-level and overfill alarms, and were these alarm systems fully operational and properly set?

q.sec: Gas (common to all vessels under IGC Code)
q.oq: Were the Master, officers, and ratings involved with cargo operations, familiar with the functions of the vessel’s cargo transfer Emergency Shut Down (ESD) systems, and was the equipment in good working order, regularly inspected, tested and maintained?

q.s: I know our ESD initiators, such as push buttons, fire detection, high level and blackout, and what they shut down. I can show the flowchart, the pre-arrival test checklist and the closing time records. Any inhibit needs authorisation and must be reinstated immediately afterwards.

q.s: Our SMS covers operation, inspection, testing and maintenance of the hatch covers, and they are in our maintenance plan. Apply soapy solution to the seals
Adjust closing devices where it leaks

Plan repair of the joint at the earliest chance
Use extra sealing only as the risk assessment allows

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for changing cargo modes, including ship-specific checklists, and were there records to show that these procedures had been followed?

Blank off suctions, droplines and gas lines
Check hatch seals and ballast spaces for gas

Inert holds and check tightness before loading

q.oq: Were the Master and all officers directly involved in cargo transfer operations familiar with the company procedure for planning cargo and ballast transfers, and were records available to demonstrate that cargo operations had been planned in accordance with the company procedure and conducted in accordance with the agreed plan?

Operations carried out that were not in the plan
Plan changed but not updated and re-approved
Records too thin to rebuild the operation; tank atmosphere or venting not as planned

Draught, trim and stress at key stages
Any COW, tank cleaning or gas freeing
Emergency stop procedure

Record the change

q.oq: Were the Master and all officers with a direct responsibility for cargo, tank cleaning or ballast operations familiar with the requirements of the ISGOTT Ship/Shore Safety Checklist (SSSCL) and, were appropriate sections of the SSSCL in use with all applicable provisions and agreements maintained throughout?

Show the record or evidence
Link it to the ISGOTT reference

A responsible officer checks the deck at least once each watch
Recorded on the SSSCL

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures which provided guidance on the level of supervision and support for cargo / port operations, and were operations supervised and supported by an appropriate team in accordance with the company procedures?

Team on duty not matching the procedure
Deck watch distracted by SIMOPS or by sounding and surveying

a: Officer on watch in CCR
Deck watch in contact by radio
Extra support for mooring and access
Senior officer if the procedure requires

pr.q: What if SIMOPS happens during cargo?
a: Extra people assigned to SIMOPS
Cargo and mooring watch not distracted
Plan states it

q.tip: Check the watch list against your plan before each stage. Do not let one rating cover moorings, gangway and sounding at once.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for checking and testing cargo and ballast system valves, and were the valves and the remote control system in satisfactory condition?

Test records with actual times and indicator checks
Emergency mode and hand pump test records
Hydraulic system at normal pressure
x: No procedure or no records of valve tests

Remote valve isolated or operated manually due to hydraulic leak
Hydraulic pressure not held during transfer or no automatic pressure keeping

q.s: Our procedure sets how often we test valves, how we time them and how we check indicators, and we record the results. I know the design times for our valves, and what to do if one is out. I can also operate the emergency mode and hand pump.

a: Report and record it
Check against ship drawings and manual
Arrange repair or adjustment
Take care for surge risk until corrected

a: Select emergency mode
Use the local hand pump
Know which valves it covers

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures for the operation, maintenance, testing, calibration and comparison of the fixed cargo tank level gauging system, and was the system in satisfactory condition and fully operational?

No risk assessment procedure for gauge failure
System inoperative or unreliable and portable gauges in use
Level alarms silenced or inhibited; officer unsure of failure actions or alarm settings
q.s: We test, calibrate and compare the fixed gauges as our procedure and the maker require, and keep records. If a gauge is unreliable we follow our risk assessed procedure to continue safely. I can show you the system and the level alarm settings.

Use portable or secondary gauging as allowed
Report the defect
Check any replacement unit is compatible and calibrated

Record the result
Calibrate as the maker's manual says

q.oq: Were the Master and deck officers familiar with the company procedure and manufacturer’s instructions for the periodic testing of the stability and loading instrument(s), and were records maintained to confirm that tests had been completed in accordance with the procedure?

Special survey test records with surveyor
Exemption certificate if no instrument is required

Instrument defective

Follow the maker's instructions
Compare to the approved results
Record it

Run a condition
Explain the result

q.s: Our loading manual and company procedure tell us about the limits on this ship, such as filling heights and free surface. They are posted in the CCR and built into our cargo plans. I can show you records that we followed them.

Evidence kept on board

pr.q: How do you know the mimic shows the true valve position?
a: Periodic checks of indicators against local position

Fault reported through defect system

Retest and adjust the brake
Record the new test
Use correct reeling and layers

Brake holding load
Reeling direction
Torque or hydraulic assist setting

Fixed and portable gas detection and fire detection
Remote controlled valves

Jacketed line drain disconnected
Fuel leakage alarm not working or not demonstrated
Spray shield missing or poor
Insulation missing, damaged or soaked in oil
Indicator cocks not capped while running
q.s: We inspect the machinery spaces on a regular PMS task using a ship-specific checklist. We look for leaks, check hoses, jacketed lines and spray shields, and make sure insulation is refitted after maintenance. I can show you the leakage alarm test.

pr.q: Which joints need spray shields?

Those near hot surfaces or ignition sources
Shield may be insulation, tape or a cover

a: Check insulation is refitted correctly
Refit spray shields and jacketed line drains
Look for leaks on restart

q.tip: Make a habit of checking oil-soaked lagging and replacing it. A wet lagging is a fire waiting to happen.

q.s: Our procedure gives the alarm set point, the actions on alarm and the test frequency. The oil mist alarm is set at not more than 5 percent of LEL, we calibrate sensors as the maker requires, and I can test it for you.

a: Not more than 5% of the lower explosive limit

Reduce engine load and stop as instructed
Do not open the crankcase until it cools

q.s: Our power packs are in a dedicated space with separate ventilation, and the doors stay closed when they run. The wire and pipe passes are sealed. Where a pack is in the open machinery space, we have an oil mist detector or an encapsulated design with a level alarm, and we test it on schedule.

It need not be watertight, but must close and be kept shut

q.tip: Check the door closer and seals during rounds. Do not wedge the door for ventilation.

q.oq: Where the vessel traded in polar waters, had the Master, Chief Mate and officers in charge of a navigational watch undertaken the additional training required by the Polar Code?
q.p: If the ship trades in polar waters, do the Master, Chief Mate and watch officers hold the extra Polar Code training certificates?
q.w: Ice and polar waters need special skills, and the wrong training can put the ship and crew at serious risk.
c: Polar Water Operational Manual section on manning and training
Basic training certificates for Master, Chief Mate and watch officers
Advanced training certificates for Master and Chief Mate
Ice navigator papers if someone else is used
rd: PWOM available onboard
Basic polar certificate for each navigating officer
Advanced polar certificate for Master and Chief Mate
Ice navigator's certificate of competency and advanced training, if used
Company ice navigator policy written down
x: PWOM does not say what extra training is needed
Master or Chief Mate has no advanced certificate and is not replaced by an ice navigator
Master or Chief Mate without even basic training
Watch officer without basic training
Ice navigator without the right certificates
q.s: Our Polar Water Operational Manual sets the training required. All watch officers hold basic polar training, and the Master and Chief Mate hold advanced training. Certificates are in the file for you to review.

pr.q: Which certificates do you need?
a: Watch officers: basic training
Master and Chief Mate: advanced training
Open water only: basic training is enough

pr.q: What if the company uses an ice navigator?
a: Master and Chief Mate then need basic training only
The ice navigator holds the advanced certificate
The arrangement is described in the procedure

q.tip: Keep copies of all polar certificates with the PWOM so you can produce them in one go.

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures to ensure the operability of the life-saving and fire-fighting systems and equipment in sub-zero temperatures, and had these procedures been complied with?
q.t: Life-saving and fire-fighting equipment in sub-zero temperatures
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures to keep lifesaving and firefighting equipment working in freezing weather, and are they followed?
q.w: Frozen lifeboats, fire lines or extinguishers fail when you need them in an emergency.
c: Company winterisation procedure and checklists
Records of periodic checks during freezing weather
Lifeboat and life raft condition, engine starting and fuel
Fire and foam line drains, extinguishers and hydrants
Eye wash stations and decontamination showers
rd: Winterisation checklist completed
Fire and foam lines drained from the lowest point with drain valve closed
Lifeboat heaters used, anti-freeze in cooling, spray system drained
Cold start instructions in the lifeboat, with the right cold start oil
Ice mallet near survival craft
Escape routes and equipment clear of snow and ice
Monitors and hydrants covered with canvas
x: No procedure or no checklist
Officer cannot find the fire or foam line drain points
Eye wash or showers not working
Insulation missing or heat tracing not working
Periodic checks not done in freezing weather
Life rafts not rated for the conditions
Lifeboat hull damage that could freeze
No cold start procedure in the lifeboat
Wrong cold start oil, wrong fuel grade, no anti-freeze
Lifeboat heaters off, doors frozen shut or spray not drained
Water or foam extinguishers left to freeze
Foam storage below zero
Equipment not ready due to ice or snow
Escape routes blocked by ice
q.s: Before reaching the cold area we used the winterisation checklist, drained the fire and foam lines and prepared the lifeboats. During the exposure we check the systems on a regular schedule and clear snow and ice from escape routes and equipment.

pr.q: How do you keep the fire main from freezing?
a: Drain from the lowest point and close the drain valve
Check the drained state by opening the drain valve
Cover monitors and hydrants

pr.q: What do you do for the lifeboat engine?
a: Use the heater and the right fuel grade
Cooling system protected with anti-freeze
Follow the posted cold start procedure

q.tip: Put the ice mallet and the cold start card where the boat crew can find them in the dark.
ref: OCIMF Large Tankers in Ice guidance

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures to ensure the operability of the engine room machinery and systems in sub-zero temperatures, and had these procedures been complied with?
q.t: Engine room machinery in sub-zero temperatures
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures to keep the engine room machinery working in freezing weather, and are they followed?
q.w: Frozen sea chests, fuel lines or hydraulics can cause loss of cooling or propulsion in ice.
c: Company winterisation procedure and checklists
Pre-entry checks of sea chests, heating systems and cooling water
While in cold: heating applied, motors running, vent flaps operated
Officer familiarity with the procedure
rd: Completed winterisation checklist
Draughts within the ice class limits
Sea chest strainers clean and steam heating on
Heating on fuel, bilge and lube oil tanks
Emergency generator heating and anti-freeze checked
Control air dry, air pipes free of ice
Stern tube oil water content checked
x: No procedure or no checklists
Officer not familiar with the procedure
Pre-entry checks not done: strainers, heating, anti-freeze, water levels
Sea chest steam heating not kept on
Space heaters not used in steering gear, battery and emergency fire pump spaces
Emergency generator room flaps or damper not closed
Not changing from heavy fuel to diesel before stopping the main engine
Hydraulic and steering motors not kept running
Ventilation flaps not operated, freshwater tanks and pipes not watched
Any winterisation equipment defective
q.s: Before entering cold waters we work through our winterisation checklist: draughts, sea chests, tank heating, emergency generator and stern tube oil. While in the cold we keep sea chest heating on, run hydraulics, use space heaters and manage ventilation so fuel lines do not chill.

pr.q: How do you protect the sea chests?
a: Clean the strainers
Keep steam heating on continuously in ice waters
Check the heating works before entering

pr.q: What do you do about fuel before stopping the main engine?
a: Change over from heavy fuel to diesel
Lines are then primed with diesel so they cannot solidify

q.tip: Start the checklist days before you reach the cold area, not on the day.
ref: OCIMF Large Tankers in Ice guidance

q.sec: Sub-zero cargo and ballast operation procedures
q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures to ensure the operability of the cargo and ballast systems in sub-zero temperatures, and had these procedures been complied with?
q.t: Cargo and ballast systems in sub-zero temperatures
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures to keep cargo and ballast systems working in freezing weather, and are they followed?
q.w: Frozen valves, vents or pumps can stop cargo operations or block pressure relief and cause damage.
c: Company winterisation procedure and checklists
Records of equipment checks before, during and after cargo operations
Deck equipment covers, greasing and drains
P/V valves, P/V breaker and deck seal heating
Officer familiarity with the procedure
rd: Completed winterisation checklist
Hydraulic cargo and COW valves covered and moved often
Valves greased with gearboxes free of water
P/V valves, mast riser and IG valves protected, checked before cargo
P/V breaker anti-freeze at the right level
Deck seal heating working and checked
Lines, heating coils, drip trays and ballast system drained as needed
x: No procedure or no winterisation checklist
Officer not familiar with the procedure
Deck lines not tested for tightness before use
Ballast water salinity not checked
Deck equipment not covered with canvas, such as P/V valves and deepwell pump motors
Valves not greased or gearboxes contain water
Deck seal heating not working
P/V breaker or stripping pump anti-freeze wrong
Lines, coils, drip trays or ballast monitor not drained
Hydraulic valves not worked often in freezing weather
Canvas covers left on ballast vents when ballasting
Records of checks missing
q.s: Before the cold area we followed our winterisation checklist: covers on deck equipment, valves greased, drains opened and anti-freeze checked. Before and during cargo we check the P/V valves, breaker and deck seal heating, and we work the hydraulic valves often so they do not freeze.

pr.q: How do you protect the P/V valves?
a: Overhaul before the cold area
Canvas covers, or steam heating
Remove covers and check for ice before cargo, with drain holes clear

pr.q: What do you check on the P/V breaker?
a: Filled with the right glycol anti-freeze mix
Level checked often
Density tested and restored after the cold weather

q.tip: Write the covers on a checklist so none are left on when you start cargo or ballast. Start hydraulic systems early.
ref: OCIMF Large Tankers in Ice guidance

q.oq: Were the Master and officers familiar with the company procedures to ensure the operability of the deck machinery, including mooring systems, in sub-zero temperatures, and had these procedures been complied with?
q.t: Deck machinery and mooring in sub-zero temperatures
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures to keep deck machinery and mooring gear working in freezing weather, and are they followed?
q.w: Ice on winches, windlasses and ropes can leave the ship unable to moor or anchor safely.
c: Company winterisation procedure and checklists
Records of checks of deck machinery during cold exposure
Hydraulic oil grade and circulation
Covers on control boxes, mooring ropes and accommodation ladder motors
Winches, windlasses and anchors proven before arrival
rd: Completed winterisation checklist
Suitable hydraulic oil, circulated when below 0 C and winches lubricated
Cranes operated and tested before cold, with cab heating checked
Main air valve to deck closed and line drained
Canvas covers on control boxes, levers and mooring ropes
Winches, windlasses and anchors proven before port
Pneumatic oil spill pumps working, if fitted
x: No procedure or checklist
Officer not familiar with the procedure
No periodic checks during sub-zero exposure
Wrong hydraulic oil grade or oil not circulated
Running winches not lubricated
Cranes not tested before the cold, crane heating not checked
Ladder motors not covered
Deck air line not drained
Control boxes and mooring ropes not covered
Winches, windlasses and anchors not proven before arrival
Equipment found frozen or iced up
q.s: Before the cold area we followed our checklist: suitable hydraulic oil, circulation, covers on controls and mooring ropes, deck air drained and cranes tested. We prove the winches and anchors before arrival and allow extra time to clear ice.

pr.q: How do you protect hydraulic machinery?
a: Check the oil grade and viscosity for the temperature
Circulate the oil when below 0 C
Lubricate winches that are left running

pr.q: How do you protect mooring ropes?
a: Canvas covers until needed
Ice crystals inside ropes damage the fibres

q.tip: Test the windlass and lower the anchors in good time before arrival when safe navigation permits, then bring them fully home before mooring.
ref: OCIMF Large Tankers in Ice guidance

q.t: Navigating in areas affected by ice
q.p: Do officers know the company procedures for navigating in ice, and have they had suitable ice training?
q.w: Ice navigation needs extra planning, watchkeeping and skills, or the ship can be damaged or beset.
c: Company procedures and checklists for ice navigation
Passage plan for the last voyage in ice
Completed checklists
Bridge log book for the last ice period
